extracted.intended_audience: landscape painters, art students, critics, and patrons interested in principles and evaluation of landscape painting
extracted.subtask_description: Principles and evaluative standards for creating and judging landscape painting, emphasizing truthful study of nature, selection and treatment of subject, composition, finish, and the moral function of art. Drawn from Ruskin's prescriptive discussion of modern and ancient landscape practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Faithful, loving study of nature
rubrics_metrics.description: An earnest, faithful, loving study of nature as she is, rejecting with abhorrence all that man has done to alter and modify her.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the primary necessity: painters should investigate and render nature itself rather than artifice. Ruskin contrasts this with the so-called 'ideal' landscapes that invent incongruities; he holds up Turner and certain English artists as those who receive 'the word of God from clouds, and leaves, and waves' and try to render the purity of impression. The study should be thorough, humble, and based on observation rather than gallery-based copying.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of the 'ideal landscape' conglomeration
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not assemble individually spoiled studies, selected so their opposing characters neutralize each other and united with unnatural violence to produce an impossible general sensation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ruskin's example of Claude's 'Il Mulino' is given: a lovely forest foreground, an incompatible herd tumbling into water, Roman soldiers on hobby-horses, a circular temple with a working water-mill built against it, ugly weirs, fishing punts, improbable cities and bridges — all jarringly juxtaposed. This anti-pattern produces an impression of the impossible and degrades art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Idealization in the right sense (knowledge-based idealizing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Idealize only by 'perfect assertion of entire knowledge of every part and character and function of the object,' not by audacious imaginative liberties that degrade nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: True idealization arises from long study and complete knowledge, and then concentrating and selecting forms to express the animating emotion. Avoid idealization that is mere invention; instead, idealize by completing details 'to the last line compatible with the dignity and simplicity of the whole.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Careful selection of subjects — perfection of kind
rubrics_metrics.description: Chosen subjects must be perfect of their kind; there is a perfection of hedgerow and cottage as well as of forest and palace.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Artists must pick subjects 'in which nature has prepared to the artist's hand the purest sources of the impression he would convey.' Humble subjects are acceptable and may yield more ideality than bombastic or unnatural elements. Avoid heaping foregrounds with colossal columns or impossible mountains when the subject cannot sustain them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concentration of studies into a single, finished picture (not casual fragments)
rubrics_metrics.description: Only that should be considered a picture in which the animating emotion of many studies is concentrated and exhibited by the aid of long-studied, painfully-chosen forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not give the world casual impressions, incomplete studies, or fleeting sketches as finished pictures. The artist must select, study, and synthesize multiple observations into a coherent, completed work; the spirit, not the raw materials, must be presented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thorough finish and industrious completion
rubrics_metrics.description: Details are to be completed to the last line compatible with dignity and simplicity; employ the noblest industry which concentrates profusion into point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Finish is not mere polishing but the patient labor that consolidates many studies into a singular, disciplined form. Ruskin warns against 'mountebank tricks of the brush' and the public's taste for quick cleverness; chaste finish requires far more knowledge and effort and should not be abandoned for marketable superficiality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not seek originality for its own sake
rubrics_metrics.description: Originality is never to be sought for its own sake — it should arise naturally out of hard, independent study of nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Originality is desirable but dangerous if pursued as a mere affectation; it must be the product of deep study. Footnote commentary acknowledges originality's necessity yet warns that it can be used for wrong ends if pretended rather than earned by knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid carelessness and mechanical copyism
rubrics_metrics.description: Reprobate careless rendering of casual impression and the mechanical copyism of unimportant subject, characterized by lightness, desultoriness, and meaningless multiplication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ruskin criticizes modern tendencies to multiply unstudied compositions and to rely on casual sketches as finished works. This habit discredits study and encourages the view that fieldwork is less valuable than studio or gallery practice. The remedy is deliberate, definitive intention and loftiness of aim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harmony of composition; reject jarring juxtapositions
rubrics_metrics.description: Composition should avoid juxtaposing incongruous elements whose characters clash; the parts must be selected and associated naturally to support the whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Il Mulino example shows how dancers, shepherds, soldiers, temples, mills, weirs, and anglers can conflict — creating ugly, monotonous or 'dead-looking' effects. Good composition selects elements that belong together in effect, line, and mood, and avoids neutralizing or degrading the impressiveness of individual studied motifs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variety without repetition across an artist's oeuvre
rubrics_metrics.description: Chosen subjects must not be repetitions of one another; each picture should be founded on a new idea and develop a totally distinct train of thought so the artist's works form a consistent, ascending series.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An artist's life-work should connect pieces from humblest scenery to most exalted, each a necessary link. Avoid producing multiple works that are essentially the same; aim for progressive distinctness and development of thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific accuracy in recording natural facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigate and arrange the facts of nature with scientific accuracy; attend to the material facts and groundwork of art before applying principles of beauty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ruskin declares the first task is hard classification of material things 'without reference to any principles of beauty or influences of emotion.' Knowledge of external characteristics — and ideally fuller scientific knowledge — underpins truthful representation; time spent multiplying crude sketches could instead build such knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use masters as comments on nature, not as authoritative models
rubrics_metrics.description: Use pictures not as authorities, but as comments on nature; avoid taking art as the final authority that stands between the artist and nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ruskin warns against slavish idolization of past masters (gallery-worship) which can lead to intellectual prostration. Study the works of Michelangelo, Raphael, Turner, etc., for instruction but not as substitutes for observing nature itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Artist's moral function and responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Art has a moral function and end; the artist should be attached with the responsibility of a preacher, influencing minds and lives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ruskin intends to show how art affects hearts and should kindle in the general mind the regard such an office demands. Avoid producing works that 'harden or degrade' rather than elevate; choose and treat subjects with moral consequence in view.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resist market-driven manufacture and superficial cleverness
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not reduce landscape painting to manufacture catering to public taste for small, clever sketches; avoid prostituting talent to the superficialness of public demand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ruskin laments that economic pressures make ten purchasers of ten-guinea sketches easier to find than one for a hundred-guinea picture, forcing artists to prefer quick bits over finished conceptions. Both artists and patrons share fault: artists who exhibit dexterity by tricks, and a public that refuses to learn to discriminate and appreciate true finish.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish painter's intellectual power from technical knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize the distinction between the painter's intellectual power (expressive language) and technical knowledge (craft), and that painting is a form of language conveying ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ruskin observes that intellectual power and technique are separable and that painting should convey thought. He notes the difficulty of fixing limits between language and thought and distinguishes decorative from expressive language; critics and artists should evaluate both content (ideas conveyed) and means (technical execution).
